summary: A proposal from the BBN authors, following an FTP meeting, for letting a user program connect two servers so a file moves directly from one to the other. It proposes a PASV command to make a server listen for the connection, along with the SOCK command. It continues RFC 438.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes commands that let a user arrange a file transfer between two FTP servers. One server listens for a connection while the other server connects to it.

subtitle: A proposal for FTP servers to establish a direct data connection.

tldr.problem: For a third-party transfer, two FTP servers need to arrange a data connection with each other.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed SOCK command supplies the other host and socket; PASV tells a server to listen for an incoming connection.
tldr.outcome: The RFC outlines a proposed server-to-server procedure discussed at an FTP meeting.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 478's status as Unknown. The RFC records a proposal for FTP server-to-server interaction.

sections.title: Server-to-Server File Transfer
sections.content:
The RFC describes a user who wants to retrieve a file from one server and send it to another. The proposed mechanism lets the two servers establish the data connection, rather than requiring the file data to pass through the user's process.

The proposal follows discussion at a recent FTP meeting at BBN.
sections.plainLanguage: A user may want to copy a file from one server to another. This proposal lets the servers carry the data between them.

sections.title: SOCK and PASV
sections.content:
The SOCK command tells a server to prepare to use a specified socket at a specified host for its data connection. The PASV command tells a server to open its data socket for listening and, after a transfer command, wait for an incoming connection.

After a positive PASV acknowledgement, an incoming request can lead the server to send a matching request, if it agrees with any earlier SOCK command.
sections.plainLanguage: SOCK tells a server which other host and socket to expect. PASV tells the server to listen for the incoming connection.

sections.title: A Transfer Sequence
sections.content:
The example has the user tell each server about the other server's data socket, then send PASV to one server. The user sends STOR to one and RTRV to the other; once PASV has been acknowledged, the transfer commands may be sent in either order.

The RFC notes that sending SOCK to the server that receives PASV allows it to check that the incoming connection is consistent with what it was told.
sections.plainLanguage: The user provides each server with the other's socket details, then asks one to listen and issues the transfer commands. The RFC says the two transfer commands can arrive in either order after the listening acknowledgement.
